analysis.one_liner: Sets federal safety standards for dams holding coal ash and other coal waste.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced weeks after a billion-gallon coal ash spill in Tennessee, drew one cosponsor, got a single subcommittee hearing, and died without ever reaching a House vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Interior Department to write safety rules for impoundments — the dams and ponds that hold coal ash, slag, and scrubber sludge — using the same engineering standards that apply to coal mine waste piles. New impoundments could not operate without meeting those standards, and Interior would have to inventory every existing one, assess the risk each poses to people and water, and issue orders to fix dangerous ones. It was introduced in January 2009, shortly after the December 2008 spill of roughly a billion gallons of coal ash from a Tennessee Valley Authority pond in Kingston, Tennessee, which buried homes and rivers nearby.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near or downstream from coal ash impoundments — typically communities around coal-fired power plants and coal mines. The bill's design, inspection, and enforcement rules would have reduced the risk of a dam failure like the Kingston spill flooding their homes or contaminating their drinking water, and the national inventory would have told them for the first time which of the hundreds of existing ponds near them were dangerous.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Interior Secretary to write design, engineering, and performance standards for the safe storage and disposal of coal ash and related wastes in impoundments, within 180 days of enactment.

Bans anyone from building or operating a coal waste impoundment anywhere except under those federal standards, and makes the existing surface mining law's inspection and penalty powers apply to violators.

Requires a national inventory of every existing impoundment, with an assessment of each dam's engineering stability and the risks it poses to surface water, groundwater, and human health, and lets the Secretary issue orders to bring dangerous existing ponds into compliance.
Lets states with approved mining programs adopt the federal rules themselves, while preserving any stronger state standards already on the books.

analysis.who_pays: Owners of coal-fired power plants and coal mining operations, who would bear the cost of engineering upgrades, inspections, and penalties for unsafe impoundments — costs likely to flow partly to electricity customers through rates. Interior would also take on the cost of writing rules and completing the national inventory.

drawbacks.text: The bill mostly grandfathers existing impoundments: the new mandatory standards apply to new ponds, while existing ones — generally the older and riskier dams — are covered only by an inventory and whatever compliance orders the Secretary chooses to issue, so the biggest threats depend on discretionary enforcement rather than a requirement.
Compliance costs for utilities would ultimately reach electricity customers in coal-heavy regions through higher rates, a cost honest supporters would acknowledge.

The bill channels the rules through the Interior Secretary under the mining law rather than through the EPA's waste program, and a good-faith objection was that an environmental and toxic-substance agency with hazardous-waste expertise is better placed to regulate coal ash disposal.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety benefit is real and targeted at a hazard the public had just watched fail catastrophically at Kingston; the main costs are compliance spending by utilities and higher power rates in coal regions, which are the ordinary price of safe waste storage. The bill's serious design weakness is the grandfathering: it hardens new impoundments but leaves the existing stock of aging ponds to discretionary orders after a risk inventory, so its protection of the most dangerous sites is partial rather than complete.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Natural Resources Committee and then to its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee, which held one hearing, and the bill sat there until the Congress ended with no committee vote and no House floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Nick Rahall of West Virginia, a Democrat, introduced the bill on January 14, 2009, weeks after the Tennessee Valley Authority's Kingston coal ash pond spill.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources on the day of introduction.
On February 4, 2009, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources.
The subcommittee held a hearing on February 12, 2009, but no further action followed; the bill never received a markup or floor vote in the 111th Congress.
The bill attracted a single cosponsor, one House Democrat.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Owners of coal-fired power plants and coal mining operations are better off, because no federal safety standards, mandatory inspections, or penalties for coal ash impoundments took effect. People living near aging ash ponds gained nothing; the hazard the bill targeted remained unaddressed by this legislation.

for.name: Rep. Nick Rahall
for.role: U.S. Representative (D-WV) and sponsor; chair of the House Natural Resources Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and got it referred to his committee and to the Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee, which held a hearing on it.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee leadership
against.role: Committee responsible for advancing the bill
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to a committee vote after the February 2009 subcommittee hearing, letting it lapse at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Coal-fired electric utilities
against.what_they_did: Opposed federal mandates governing the design and operation of coal ash storage ponds during this period, as the industry publicly fought federal coal ash disposal rules for years.

sides.party_line_note: There were no committee or floor votes, and the bill's only recorded support came from its Democratic sponsor and a single Democratic cosponsor, so no partisan pattern of support or opposition shows up in the record.

industries.note: Utilities own and operate the ash ponds and impoundments the bill regulates; they would have faced federal design standards, inspections, and penalties, with costs passed partly to ratepayers. Their interest in avoiding those costs ran against the safety of nearby communities.

The bill treats coal waste impoundments like surface coal mining operations under the 1977 mining law, exposing them to its inspection and penalty regime, but it largely exempts existing impoundments from the new standards, softening the burden. Coal waste dams are among the structures the standards would govern.

A national inventory, dam assessments, and mandated redesign or remediation of impoundments would have created work for firms that assess and stabilize waste dams. Safer impoundments are the same outcome communities near them want.
